title: Chapter 35 — The Mast-Head
paragraphs: It was during the more pleasant weather that my first turn at the masthead came around, in due rotation with the other seamen.

On most American whalers, the mastheads are manned almost as soon as the ship leaves port, even though she may have fifteen thousand miles or more to sail before reaching her proper cruising ground. And if, after a three, four, or five-year voyage, she's heading home with anything unfilled — even an empty vial — then her mastheads stay manned to the last. Not until her very topmost poles sail in among the port's church spires does she give up the hope of catching one more whale.

Now, since the business of standing mastheads, whether on land or at sea, is very ancient and interesting, let us dwell on it a while. I believe the earliest masthead-standers were the old Egyptians, because in all my research I find no one who came before them. Though their predecessors, the builders of Babel, must certainly have intended their tower to be the tallest masthead in all Asia or Africa, that great stone mast went by the board in the terrible gale of God's wrath before the final piece was put on top. So we can't give those Babel builders priority over the Egyptians. And that the Egyptians were a nation of masthead-standers is supported by the common belief among archaeologists that the first pyramids were built for astronomical purposes — a theory nicely supported by the stair-like formation of all four sides, by which those old astronomers would climb to the summit with prodigious leg-stretches and call out for new stars, just as the lookouts on a modern ship call out for a sail or a whale. In Saint Stylites, the famous early Christian hermit who built himself a tall stone pillar in the desert and spent the rest of his life on top of it, hauling up his food from the ground — in him we have a remarkable example of a dauntless masthead-stander, who wouldn't be driven from his post by fog, frost, rain, hail, or sleet, but bravely faced everything to the end, literally dying at his post. Of modern masthead-standers we have only a lifeless set: statues of stone, iron, and bronze who, though capable of withstanding a stiff gale, are completely useless at the business of calling out when they spot something. There is Napoleon, standing atop the column of Vendome, arms folded, some hundred and fifty feet in the air, unconcerned about who rules the decks below. Great Washington, too, stands high on his towering mast in Baltimore, and like one of Hercules' pillars, his column marks the point of human greatness beyond which few mortals will go. Admiral Nelson also stands his masthead on a gun-metal capstan in Trafalgar Square. Even when obscured by London smoke, the sign is still there that a hidden hero stands above — for where there's smoke, there must be fire. But neither great Washington, nor Napoleon, nor Nelson will answer a single call from below, however desperately invoked for their counsel by the troubled decks they look down upon — however much we might suppose their spirits can see through the thick haze of the future and spot what dangers must be avoided.

It may seem wrong to compare the masthead-standers on land with those at sea, but they're not so different, as demonstrated by a detail for which Obed Macy, the sole historian of Nantucket, is our source. Worthy Obed tells us that in the early days of the whale fishery, before ships were regularly sent out in pursuit, the islanders erected tall poles along the coast, to which lookouts climbed by means of nailed rungs, like chickens going up stairs in a henhouse. A few years ago, the same system was adopted by the bay whalemen of New Zealand, who, upon spotting whales, signaled the waiting boats near the beach. But this custom is now obsolete. So let us turn to the proper masthead: that of a whale ship at sea. The three mastheads are manned from sunrise to sunset, the sailors taking regular turns (as at the helm) and relieving each other every two hours. In the calm weather of the tropics, the masthead is delightful — especially for a dreamy, meditative man. There you stand, a hundred feet above the silent decks, striding across the deep as if the masts were giant stilts. Beneath you and between your legs, so to speak, swim the largest monsters of the sea, just as ships once sailed between the legs of the famous Colossus of Rhodes. There you stand, lost in the infinite expanse of the ocean, with nothing stirred but the waves. The hypnotized ship lazily rolls. The drowsy trade winds blow. Everything dissolves you into lethargy. For the most part, in this tropical whaling life, a sublime uneventfulness wraps around you. You hear no news. You read no newspapers. No extras with alarming reports of ordinary events trick you into unnecessary excitement. You hear of no family troubles or bankrupt investments or falling stocks. You never worry about what to have for dinner — all your meals for three years or more are neatly stowed in barrels, and your menu is fixed.

On one of those southern whalers, on a long three or four-year voyage, as often happens, the total hours you spend at the masthead would add up to several entire months. And it is a great pity that the place where you devote such a large portion of your natural life should be so completely lacking in anything cozy or comfortable — so poorly suited to creating any sense of domestic warmth, like a bed, a hammock, a coffin, a sentry box, a pulpit, a coach, or any other of those snug little enclosures in which men temporarily shut themselves away. Your usual perch is the head of the topgallant mast, where you stand on two thin parallel sticks (found almost only on whalers) called the topgallant cross-trees. Here, tossed about by the sea, the beginner feels about as comfortable as he would standing on a bull's horns. In cold weather you can carry your house aloft in the form of a watch-coat, but strictly speaking the thickest watch-coat is no more a house than the naked body. For just as the soul is glued inside its fleshly dwelling and can't freely move about in it, or even leave it, without risking death (like an ignorant traveler crossing the snowy Alps in winter), so a watch-coat is not so much a house as just another layer of skin. You can't put shelves or drawers in your body, and no more can you make a closet out of your coat.

On this subject, it is greatly to be regretted that the mastheads of southern whale ships are not provided with those wonderful little tents or platforms called crow's-nests, which protect the lookouts of Greenland whalers from the brutal weather of the frozen seas. In the fireside narrative of Captain Sleet, titled A Voyage Among the Icebergs, in Quest of the Greenland Whale, and Incidentally for the Re-discovery of the Lost Icelandic Colonies of Old Greenland, all masthead-standers are treated to a charmingly detailed account of the then recently invented crow's-nest aboard the Glacier, which was Captain Sleet's ship. He called it Sleet's Crow's-Nest in honor of himself, being the original inventor and patentee, and free from all ridiculous false modesty. He held that if we name our children after ourselves (we fathers being the original inventors), we should likewise name any other apparatus we create. In shape, the crow's-nest is something like a large barrel — open at the top but fitted with a movable side-screen to shield your head from the wind in a gale. Being fixed atop the mast, you climb into it through a small trap-hatch in the bottom. On the after side there's a comfortable seat with a locker underneath for umbrellas, scarves, and coats. In front is a leather rack for your speaking trumpet, pipe, telescope, and other nautical necessities. When Captain Sleet stood his own masthead in this crow's-nest, he tells us he always had a rifle with him (also in the rack), along with powder flask and shot, for popping off stray narwhals or vagrant sea-unicorns in those waters — you can't shoot them successfully from the deck because of the water's resistance, but shooting down at them is quite another thing. Now, it was clearly a labor of love for Captain Sleet to describe all the detailed comforts of his crow's-nest. And though he gives us a very scientific account of his experiments there with a small compass he kept for correcting the errors caused by what's called the "local attraction" of the ship's iron — I say, though the Captain is very careful and scientific about his "compass deviations" and "approximate errors," he knows perfectly well that he was not so absorbed in those deep magnetic studies as to fail reaching for that well-stocked little case-bottle tucked neatly within arm's reach in one corner of his crow's-nest. Though on the whole I greatly admire and even love the brave, honest, learned Captain, I hold it very much against him that he so completely ignores that bottle, seeing what a faithful friend and comfort it must have been while, with mittened fingers and hooded head, he was studying mathematics up there in that bird's nest within three or four perches of the pole.

But if we southern whale-fishers aren't as snugly housed aloft as Captain Sleet and his Greenlanders were, that disadvantage is greatly offset by the wonderfully serene weather of those seductive seas where we mostly sail. For one, I used to lounge up the rigging quite leisurely, resting in the top for a chat with Queequeg or anyone else off duty I might find there. Then I'd climb a little higher, throw a lazy leg over the topsail yard, take a preliminary survey of the watery pastures, and at last reach my final destination.

Let me make a clean confession here and frankly admit that I kept a poor watch. With the problem of the universe revolving in my head, how could I — left completely alone at such a thought-provoking altitude — how could I take seriously my duty to observe all whale-ship standing orders: "Keep your weather eye open and sing out every time."

And let me right here give a solemn warning to you ship-owners of Nantucket! Beware of enlisting in your watchful fisheries any young man with a lean brow and hollow eye, given to untimely philosophizing, who offers to ship with Plato instead of Bowditch in his head. Beware of such a one, I say. Your whales must be seen before they can be killed, and this sunken-eyed young philosopher will tow you ten times around the world and never make you one pint of sperm oil richer. Nor are these warnings unnecessary. For nowadays, the whale fishery serves as a refuge for many romantic, melancholy, and absent-minded young men, disgusted with the grinding cares of life on land and seeking feeling in tar and blubber. Childe Harold not infrequently perches himself on the masthead of some unlucky, disappointed whale ship and, in moody tones, declaims:
"Roll on, thou deep and dark blue ocean, roll! Ten thousand blubber-hunters sweep over thee in vain."

Very often the captains of such ships scold these absent-minded young philosophers, criticizing them for not taking enough "interest" in the voyage — hinting that they are so hopelessly lost to all honorable ambition that they would secretly rather not see whales at all. But it's useless. These young Platonists have a theory that their vision is imperfect. They are nearsighted. What use, then, to strain their eyes? They've left their opera glasses at home.

"Why, you monkey," said a harpooner to one of these lads, "we've been cruising now hard on three years, and you haven't spotted a whale yet. Whales are as scarce as hen's teeth whenever you're up here." Perhaps they were. Or perhaps there might have been whole schools of them on the far horizon. But lulled into such an opium-like daze of vacant, unconscious daydreaming is this absent-minded youth — by the blending rhythm of waves and thoughts — that at last he loses his identity. He takes the mystic ocean at his feet for the visible image of that deep, blue, bottomless soul pervading all mankind and nature. Every strange, half-glimpsed, gliding, beautiful thing that escapes him, every dimly perceived rising fin of some unidentifiable form, seems to him the embodiment of those elusive thoughts that populate the soul by continually flitting through it. In this enchanted state, your spirit ebbs away to where it came from, becoming diffused through time and space, like scattered ashes forming at last a part of every shore around the globe.

There is no life in you now, except the rocking life given by a gently rolling ship — borrowed from the sea, and by the sea from the unfathomable tides of God. But while this sleep, this dream is upon you, move your foot or hand an inch — slip your grip even slightly — and your identity comes rushing back in horror. Over spiraling vortexes you hover. And perhaps, at midday, in the fairest weather, with one half-strangled shriek you drop through that transparent air into the summer sea, never to rise again. Take heed, you Pantheists!
